To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cochlear reflectance, a noninvasive probe of inner ear function, is a function of stimulus level that has multiple peaks in the time domain.

the cochlea contributes measurably to ear-canal reflectivity, that the magnitude of this contribution decreases with increasing level, and that it has multiple peaks in the envelope of the time domain.
the cochlear reflectance is the inner- ear contribution to the ear-canal reflectivity measured in the ear-canal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing new methods to measure the inner ear's contribution to ear canal reflectance.
the measurement and characterization of cochlear reflectance in humans.
understanding the mechanisms of OAE generation and the use of OAEs as a tool to assess cochlear function and disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cochlear reflectance measurement is a new and potentially important tool in the study of cochlear function and disease.
the cochlear reflectance measurement has the potential to become an important tool in assessing the status of the human cochlea, similar to other otoacoustic emissions measurements.
CR is the inner- ear contribution to the total ear-canal reflectivity, which is the ratio of the reverse- to the forward-propagating sound pressure measured in a closed ear canal.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that the cochlea is a reflector, that the reflectance magnitude is dependent upon the stimulus level, that the reflectivity is not constant across the frequency range, and that the reflectivity changes with age.
CR measurements can provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying OAE generation, as well as provide information about the status of the inner ear.
CR is a new measurement of the inner-ear response to a wide-band noise probe that is similar to other OEA measurements in its ability to probe cochlear function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cochlea reflects a measurable fraction of the sound pressure incident on the eardrum and that the cochlear reflectance is a function of stimulus level and frequency.
CR can be measured in humans with high bandwidth, high signal-to-noise ratio, and minimal influence of the measurement hardware.
the cochlea is a complex system with multiple components, and the OAE reflects the interaction of these components.
